Architecture

Mughal architecture: features, phases and key buildings

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Mughal architecture is the building style of the Mughal emperors in the 16th and 17th centuries. It blends Persian and Central Asian ideas with Indian craft: double domes, large arched gateways, charbagh gardens, red sandstone and white marble, pietra dura inlay and strict symmetry. Key examples are Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort.

Talaash Heritage runs walks at Humayun's Tomb, the Red Fort and Safdarjung's Tomb, and Golden Triangle journeys with an archaeologist.

Features of Mughal architecture

Mughal buildings are easy to recognise once you know a handful of features. Most of them came from Timurid Central Asia and Persia, but were built by Indian masons and craftsmen who added local forms and skills.

  • Symmetry and axial planning: buildings and gardens laid out on clear central lines.
  • Charbagh: a four-part garden divided by water channels and walkways, often with a tomb at the centre.
  • Double dome: an inner dome for the interior and a taller outer dome for the skyline.
  • Iwan and pishtaq: a large vaulted arch set in a rectangular frame on the facade.
  • Materials: red sandstone in the earlier phase, white marble in the later.
  • Chhatris and chhajjas: small domed kiosks and deep sloping eaves, both Indian forms.
  • Decoration: pietra dura (stone inlay), carved floral panels, calligraphy, jali screens.

Mughal architecture under Akbar

Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, built in the 1560s and 1570s, is the first great Mughal garden tomb. Commissioned by Humayun's widow Bega Begum and designed by the architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, it set the pattern later taken to its height at the Taj: a raised platform, a double dome and a charbagh. A walk around Humayun's Tomb is the best introduction to the style.

At Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's short-lived capital near Agra, the buildings are mostly red sandstone with flat beams, brackets and pillars drawn from Gujarati and Rajasthani building, combined with Persian arches. The Buland Darwaza, the Jama Masjid and the Panch Mahal show this mixture. Our session on Fatehpur Sikri's Mughal urban vision looks at the city as a whole.

Mughal architecture under Shah Jahan

Shah Jahan's reign is often called the high point. The Taj Mahal at Agra, built as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal from about 1632, uses white Makrana marble, pietra dura inlay of coloured stones, and calligraphy that seems to stay the same size as it rises up the arches. The tomb sits at the river end of the garden, not in its centre, an unusual choice that frames it against the sky.

In Delhi he founded Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort, completed in 1648, and the Jama Masjid. Inside the fort, the Diwan-i-Am and Diwan-i-Khas show marble pavilions with cusped arches and inlay. A visit to the Red Fort Complex and Jama Masjid covers this phase in one morning.

Mughal gardens and later Mughal buildings

Gardens were central. The charbagh was an image of order, with water, shade and fruit trees, and it framed tombs, palaces and pleasure retreats. The Shalimar and Nishat gardens in Kashmir, Pinjore in Haryana and Roshanara Bagh in Delhi show different versions.

After Aurangzeb, building continued on a smaller scale. Safdarjung's Tomb in Delhi, from the 1750s, is often called the last great Mughal garden tomb. Its proportions are taller and its decoration plainer than Humayun's Tomb, which makes the two a useful pair to compare.

Mughal ideas also spread beyond imperial projects. Rajput rulers at Amber, Jaipur and Orchha adopted Mughal arches, gardens and audience halls, mixing them with their own palace traditions, and nobles across north India built smaller tombs, sarais and mosques in the imperial manner. That spread is one reason the style became so widely recognised.

Mughal architecture: notes for students

  • Period: 1526 to the mid 18th century, peak under Akbar and Shah Jahan.
  • Origins: Timurid and Persian, built with Indian craft and forms.
  • Key features: charbagh, double dome, iwan, chhatri, red sandstone and white marble, pietra dura.
  • First great garden tomb: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi (UNESCO, 1993).
  • UNESCO Mughal sites: Agra Fort and Taj Mahal (1983), Fatehpur Sikri (1986), Humayun's Tomb (1993), Red Fort Complex (2007).
  • Mughal architecture is a later chapter of the wider tradition of Indo-Islamic architecture.

Questions people ask

What are the main features of Mughal architecture?

Symmetrical planning, charbagh gardens, bulbous double domes, large arched gateways, chhatris, red sandstone and white marble, pietra dura inlay, jali screens and calligraphy. It combines Persian and Central Asian ideas with Indian building craft and forms.

Which is the first Mughal building in India?

Babur built gardens and a few mosques, such as the Kabuli Bagh mosque at Panipat, soon after 1526. The first great Mughal monument, which set the pattern for later tombs, is Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, built in the 1560s and 1570s.

Why is Shah Jahan's period called the golden age of Mughal architecture?

Under Shah Jahan, Mughal building reached its most refined form: white marble, precise symmetry and fine pietra dura inlay. The Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid in Delhi were all built in his reign.

What is the difference between Mughal and Indo-Islamic architecture?

Indo-Islamic architecture is the broader tradition that began with the Delhi Sultanate around 1200. Mughal architecture is one later phase of it, from 1526 onward, with its own features such as charbagh tombs, double domes and white marble with pietra dura.
